claim: Working memory (WM) capacity is limited.
source: It has long been appreciated that WM capacity is limited, but despite many decades of research, the nature of these limitations remains controversial.
evidence: This is established scientific consensus referenced in the introduction.

claim: Miller (1956) posited that WM is limited to roughly seven items.
source: For example, early work by Miller, 1956 famously posited that WM is limited to roughly seven items, but he also stated that the precise limitation might vary depending on the information quantity of the relevant memoranda.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miller, 1956.

claim: The 'slots' theory argues that WM is limited to a specific number of items (roughly four items).
source: The 'slots' theory argues that WM is limited to a specific number of items. According to this account, each item is stored in a discrete slot and encoded with high precision, leading to low or zero errors when that item is probed at recall. When the number of items to be remembered exceeds the capacity (roughly four items; Cowan, 2008), some items will be forgotten, and therefore participants resort to guessing (Zhang and Luck, 2008; Fukuda et al., 2010; Luck and Vogel, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature on slots theory.

claim: The 'resource' theory argues that people can store an arbitrarily large number of items in WM with no inherent item limit, but precision decreases with each added item.
source: In contrast, the 'resource' theory argues that people can store an arbitrarily large number of items in WM, with no inherent item limit, but that each item competes for a shared pool of resources. As a result, the precision of each memoranda goes down with each added item to be recalled. In the limit, when many items are presented, each one is recalled with low precision, which can masquerade as guessing (Bays et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to resource theory literature.

claim: Individual differences in WM capacity are largely determined by one's ability to filter out distracting items.
source: For example, individual differences in WM capacity are largely determined not by the raw number of items one can store but rather one's ability to filter out distracting items (Vogel et al., 2005; McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Astle et al., 2014; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Vogel, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Effective WM capacity can fluctuate depending on stimulus complexity, sensory modality, and experience with the stimuli.
source: More generally, one can leverage various (potentially unconscious) memory strategies to improve 'effective capacity,' leading to experimentally observed capacity measurements that fluctuate depending on stimulus complexity, sensory modality, and experience with the stimuli (Pusch et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Pusch et al., 2023.

claim: Information stored in WM can be partitioned into discrete representations, with similar items stored in a shared partition (chunking).
source: For example, recent theoretical and empirical work suggested that information stored in WM can be partitioned into discrete representations, but that similar items could be stored in a shared partition, in effect chunking them together (Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nassar et al., 2018.

claim: Active chunking strategy serves as a lossy information compression mechanism that frees up space for other items at the cost of reducing precision for chunked items.
source: This active chunking strategy serves as a lossy information compression mechanism: it frees up space for other items to be stored and recalled. This happens at the cost of reducing precision for the chunked items.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the mechanism of chunking, supported by inference from the cited work.

claim: The optimal chunking criterion varies systematically with set size and can be acquired via reinforcement learning.
source: Moreover, (Nassar et al., 2018) showed that the optimal chunking criterion (i.e. how similar two items need to be to merit storing as a single chunk) varies systematically with set size (number of items to be remembered) and can be acquired via reinforcement learning (RL).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nassar et al., 2018.

claim: Humans adapted chunking on a trial-by-trial basis as a function of reward feedback.
source: In line with this account, they reported evidence that humans adapted chunking on a trial-by-trial basis as a function of reward feedback in their experiment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nassar et al., 2018 (implied by 'they').

claim: Optimal performance in VWM was associated with more chunking with increasing set size.
source: They also performed a meta-analysis of other visual working memory (VWM) datasets showed that optimal performance was associated with more chunking with increasing set size.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nassar et al., 2018 (implied by 'they').

claim: The dominant neural model of visual working memory is the ring attractor model of prefrontal cortex.
source: The dominant neural model of visual working memory is the ring attractor model of prefrontal cortex (PFC), whereby multiple items can be maintained via persistent activity in attractor states (Edin et al., 2009; Wei et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ring attractor models.

claim: In ring attractor models, nearby attractors coding for overlapping visual stimuli can collide, leading to chunking and loss of precision.
source: In these models, nearby attractors coding for overlapping visual stimuli can collide, leading to a form of chunking and loss of precision, and where some items are forgotten due to lateral inhibition (Wei et al., 2012; Almeida et al., 2015; Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to ring attractor models.

claim: Previous ring attractor models cannot determine whether or not an item should be stored and cannot filter content to only include relevant information.
source: Firstly, these models cannot determine whether or not an item should be stored. In other words, unlike humans (Vogel et al., 2005; McNab and Klingberg, 2008), they cannot improve effective capacity by filtering content to only include relevant information.
evidence: This is a limitation identified by the authors based on comparison with human data.

claim: Chunking in previous ring attractor models is obligatory and cannot be adapted with task demands.
source: Second, any chunking that occurs in these models is obligatory – determined only by how overlapping the neural populations are and hence whether attractors will collide. Thus, chunking can't be adapted with task demands as required by normative models and human data (Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a limitation identified by the authors based on comparison with normative models and human data.

claim: Previous ring attractor models cannot select a specific item from memory based on a probe during recall.
source: Finally, during recall, these network models cannot select a specific item from memory based on a probe (accuracy in these models is considered high as long as the relevant stimulus is encoded somewhere in the pool of neurons; Edin et al., 2009; Wei et al., 2012; Almeida et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation identified by the authors based on analysis of previous models.

claim: Limitations in WM capacity have been linked to difficulty in binding items to their respective slots in memory.
source: Indeed, limitations in WM capacity have been linked to difficulty in binding items to their respective slots in memory (Oberauer, 2013; Oberauer and Lin, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oberauer's work.

claim: Selective updating of information in memory slots produces a recency bias in human WM.
source: Moreover, the selective updating of information in these slots is thought to produce a recency bias ubiquitously observed in human WM (Oberauer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oberauer et al., 2012.

claim: PBWM models focus on how interactions between basal ganglia, thalamus, and PFC support independent updating of separable PFC 'stripes'.
source: Another complementary line of biologically-inspired neural network models addresses how interactions between basal ganglia (BG), thalamus, and PFC support independent updating of separable PFC 'stripes' (anatomical clusters of interconnected neurons that are isolated from other stripes; Levitt et al., 1993; Pucak et al., 1996; Frank et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to PBWM models and anatomical studies.

claim: PBWM models simulate the brain's decision whether to encode a sensory item in WM (selective input gating).
source: These prefrontal cortex basal ganglia working memory (PBWM) models focus on the aforementioned 'management' and variable binding problem. They simulate the brain's decision whether to encode a sensory item in WM ('selective input gating').
evidence: This is a description of PBWM model functionality supported by citations.

claim: PBWM models simulate which item stored in WM should be accessed for reporting or subsequent processing (output gating).
source: They also simulate which item (of those stored in WM) should be accessed ('output gating') for reporting or subsequent processing (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Hazy et al., 2007; Krueger and Dayan, 2009; Stocco et al., 2010; Frank and Badre, 2012; Kriete et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of PBWM model functionality supported by citations.

claim: PBWM networks learn effective gating policies via dopaminergic reinforcement learning signaling in the BG.
source: Via dopaminergic reinforcement learning signaling in the BG, the networks learn an effective gating policy for a given WM task (Frank and Badre, 2012).
evidence: This is a description of PBWM learning mechanism supported by citation.

claim: The basal ganglia contributes to filtering (input gating) of WM, which improves effective capacity.
source: The PBWM framework also accords with multiple lines of empirical evidence, ranging from neuroimaging to manipulation studies, suggesting that the BG contributes to filtering (input gating) of WM (which improves effective capacity) (McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Cools et al., 2007; Cools et al., 2010; Baier et al., 2010; Nyberg and Eriksson, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: The basal ganglia contributes to selecting among items held in WM (output gating).
source: and selecting among items held in WM (output gating; Chatham et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chatham et al., 2014.

claim: Striatal DA alters WM gating policies analogous to its impact on motor RL.
source: Evidence also supports the PBWM prediction that striatal DA alters WM gating policies analogous to its impact on motor RL (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Moustafa et al., 2008); for review see Frank and Fossella, 2011.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies and a review.

claim: Striatum and thalamus are needed to support WM maintenance, gating, and switching in rodent models.
source: Finally, these human studies are complemented by causal manipulations in rodent models implicating both striatum and thalamus as needed to support WM maintenance, gating, and switching (Rikhye et al., 2018; Nakajima et al., 2019; Wilhelm et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to rodent studies.

claim: Previous PBWM models have only been applied to WM tasks with discrete stimuli and have not addressed the tradeoff between precision and recall in VWM.
source: However, to date, these PBWM models have only been applied to WM tasks with discrete stimuli and thus have not addressed the tradeoff between precision and recall in VWM.
evidence: This is a limitation identified by the authors based on review of previous PBWM applications.

claim: The authors modified PBWM to accommodate continuous representations used in the delayed report color wheel task.
source: We modified PBWM to accommodate continuous representations such as those used in the delayed report color wheel task (van den Berg et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2018), see Figure 2a common task to assess precision and recall characteristics of VWM and which forms the main basis for our simulations.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the authors' model modifications.

claim: The authors represented color for each stimulus as randomly varying from 0 to 2pi using a population code.
source: To simulate continuous report tasks, we represented the color for each stimulus as randomly varying from 0 to 2pi using a population code, where each neuron in the layer maximally responds for a particular color, and the full representation for a given continuous input is represented as a Gaussian bump over an average of 10 neurons in a 20 neuron layer.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model implementation.

claim: The chunk-augmented PBWM network outperforms control models that lack chunking abilities across a range of task conditions.
source: Notably, we find that this chunk-augmented PBWM network outperforms control models that lack chunking abilities across a range of task conditions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the model simulations presented in the results.

claim: Chunk models outperform control networks even when control models are endowed with an allocated capacity that exceeds the set size.
source: Chunk models outperform control networks even when the control models are endowed with an allocated capacity that exceeds the set size.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the model simulations presented in the results.

claim: The performance advantage of chunk models stems from a credit assignment problem that arises when networks must learn to store and access multiple items in WM.
source: This latter result stems from a credit assignment problem that arises when networks must learn to store and access multiple items in WM.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results based on analysis of learning dynamics.

claim: Chunking allows for a common set of stripes to be repeatedly reused and reinforced, limiting the number of possible solutions explored.
source: Chunking instead allows for a common set of stripes to be repeatedly reused and reinforced, limiting the number of possible solutions explored.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model mechanism based on analysis of gating policies.

claim: The model results lend insight into a normative rationale for why WM capacity is limited in the first place.
source: As such, this result lends insight into a normative rationale for why WM capacity is limited in the first place.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model results.

claim: The model suggests a computational rather than anatomical limit to WM capacity.
source: These simulations also suggest a computational rather than anatomical limit to WM capacity.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model results.

claim: The model shows a recency bias, with increased accuracy for reporting items presented more recently.
source: Finally, we show that, like humans, the model shows a recency bias, with increased accuracy for reporting items that had been presented more recently.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The recency bias results from an increased propensity to update items presented earlier and as a consequence of chunking of earlier items.
source: This results both from an increased propensity to update items that had been presented earlier and as a consequence of chunking of earlier items.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism underlying the recency bias in the model.

claim: The model's account of recency effects is consistent with evidence in the human literature and inconsistent with alternative neural models of passive decay.
source: This account is consistent with evidence in the human literature on the nature of recency effects Oberauer et al., 2012, and inconsistent with alternative neural models of passive decay.
evidence: This is a comparison of the model's predictions with human data and alternative models.

claim: The model is implemented using an updated version of the Leabra framework written in the Go programming language.
source: The model is implemented using an updated version of the Leabra framework (O'Reilly et al., 2024), written in the Go programming language (see https://github.com/emer/emergent, copy archived at emer, 2025).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model implementation.

claim: Leabra uses point neurons with excitatory, inhibitory, and leak conductances contributing to an integrated membrane potential.
source: Leabra uses point neurons with excitatory, inhibitory, and leak conductances contributing to an integrated membrane potential, which is then thresholded and transformed to produce a rate code output communicated to other units.
evidence: This is a description of the Leabra framework.

claim: The PBWM model is built based on research surrounding WM, gating, and RL developed over a series of articles.
source: The PBWM model (Figure 1) is built based on a large repertoire of research surrounding WM, gating, and RL and has been developed over a series of articles (see introduction).
evidence: This is a statement about the model's foundation in prior research.

claim: The authors modified PBWM to accommodate continuous representations throughout the network (input, PFC, and response layers).
source: Here, we focus on the high level description of its functionality and the unique additions to the current application, particularly the implementation of continuous rather than discrete representations throughout the network (input, PFC, and response layers), and the chunking mechanism.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model modifications.

claim: In the color wheel task, participants are presented with multiple colored bars where each bar has a color and orientation.
source: In this task, participants are presented with multiple colored bars on a visual display where each bar has two attributes: a color and orientation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: After a delay in the color wheel task, participants are shown one of the orientations in gray and must report the associated color using a continuous color wheel.
source: After some delay, participants are shown only one of the orientations in gray, and the subject's task is to report the color that was associated with that orientation using a continuous color wheel.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task.

claim: The authors represented color as a Gaussian bump over an average of 10 neurons in a 20 neuron layer.
source: To simulate continuous report tasks, we represented the color for each stimulus as randomly varying from 0 to 2pi using a population code, where each neuron in the layer maximally responds for a particular color, and the full representation for a given continuous input is represented as a Gaussian bump over an average of 10 neurons in a 20 neuron layer.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model implementation.

claim: The stimuli are presented sequentially to the model to simplify the binding problem, mimic a sequential attentional mechanism, and make contact with literature on serial WM tasks.
source: The stimuli are presented sequentially to the mode. This serves three purposes: to simplify the binding problem, to mimic a sequential attentional mechanism, and to make contact with literature on serial WM tasks
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model design.

claim: Sequential presentation of stimuli makes the model vulnerable to serial dependence in its chunking, consistent with that observed empirically.
source: This also makes the model vulnerable to serial dependence it its chunking, consistent with that observed empirically, whereby WM reports are biased towards the last stimulus that was presented Bliss et al., 2017; Kiyonaga et al., 2017; Fischer and Whitney, 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The PFC is divided into superficial and deep layers in the PBWM model.
source: As in prior PBWM models, the PFC is divided into superficial and deep layers (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Hazy et al., 2007; Frank and Badre, 2012; Hazy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture supported by citations.

claim: Superficial PFC layers transiently reflect input stimuli as candidates to be considered for storage in WM.
source: The superficial PFC layers for each stripe will always reflect the input stimuli transiently, as candidates to be considered for storage in WM.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: For stimuli to be maintained robustly over delays, they have to be gated into WM.
source: But for these stimuli to be maintained robustly over delays (and over intervening other stimuli on subsequent time points), they have to be gated into WM.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: When there is relatively more Go than NoGo activity in a BG module, the corresponding Thalamic output unit is activated, triggering robust maintenance in deep PFC layers.
source: When there is relatively more Go than NoGo activity in a given module, the corresponding Thalamic output unit is activated, inducing thalamocortical reverberation and activation of intrinsic ionic maintenance currents, thereby triggering robust maintenance of information in the deep PFC maintenance layers (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Hazy et al., 2007; Frank and Badre, 2012; Hazy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Only the stripes that have been input-gated continue to maintain the most recent color representation in an attractor over time.
source: Thus only the stripes that have been input-gated continue to maintain the most recent color representation in an attractor over time.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Gating in PBWM implements a form of 'role-addressable' memory where decisions about which stripe to gate into depend on its assigned role.
source: Importantly, gating in PBWM implements a form of 'role-addressable' memory: the decisions about whether and which stripe to gate colors into depends on its assigned role. In this case, the orientation probe associated with the color determines where it should be gated.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: The PBWM stripes serve a variable binding function which can be linked to key/query coding.
source: Thus, the PBWM stripes serve a variable binding function (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006) which can also be linked to key/query coding (Traylor et al., 2024; Swan and Wyble, 2014): in this case, the network can learn to use the orientations to guide which stripe is accessed, and the population within the stripe represents the content (color).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism supported by citations.

claim: During recall, the network uses a gating policy to output gate the stripe corresponding to the probed orientation.
source: During a recall trial, the network is presented with only a single orientation probe. The model needs to correctly 'output gate:' select from multiple PFC maintenance stripes, so that only a single representation is activated in the corresponding PFC 'output stripes,' which in turn projects to the output layer (Figure 3 bottom row).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Rewards were given in a continuously linear fashion based on the difference between output and the target color.
source: Rewards were given in a continuously linear fashion based on the difference between output and the target color. The activity of the output neurons was decoded (using a weighted linear combination of neuron activities; Almeida et al., 2015) and the reward given was inversely proportional with the error.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model training.

claim: Correctly recalling a color requires having it stored in PFC and reading out from the correct stripe that corresponds to the probed item.
source: Correctly recalling a color thus requires not only having it stored in PFC, but reading out from the correct stripe that corresponds to the probed item.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Successful performance requires learning both proper input gating strategies and output gating strategies.
source: Note that successful performance in this and other WM tasks (Hazy et al., 2007; Frank and Badre, 2012) requires learning both the proper input gating strategies (which PFC stripes to gate information into, depending on the orientation, and which to continue to maintain during intervening items), and output gating strategies (which PFC stripes to read out from in response to a particular orientation probe).
evidence: This is a description of the model learning requirements supported by citations.

claim: Learning is acquired via reinforcement learning mediated by dopaminergic signals projecting to the striatum.
source: Such learning is acquired via reinforcement learning mediated by dopaminergic signals projecting to the striatum (represented by the bottom half of the model).
evidence: This is a description of the model learning mechanism.

claim: At recall, the network receives a dopamine burst or dip conveying a reward prediction error signal.
source: At the time of recall, the network receives a dopamine (DA) burst or dip conveying a reward prediction error signal (RPE, by comparing the reward it receives with the reward it expected to receive using a Rescorla Wagner delta rule algorithm).
evidence: This is a description of the model learning mechanism.

claim: DA signals are used to modulate synaptic plasticity in the Go and NoGo units, reinforcing adaptive gating operations.
source: These DA signals are used to modulate synaptic plasticity in the Go and NoGo units, reinforcing corticostriatal Go signals that drive adaptive input and output gating operations (following positive RPEs), and reinforcing NoGo units that suppress ineffective gating strategies (following negative RPEs).
evidence: This is a description of the model learning mechanism.

claim: The model's previous gating decisions are flagged using an eligibility trace via synaptic tagging.
source: The model's previous gating decisions are flagged using an eligibility trace via synaptic tagging. Thus, Rewards modulate Go and NoGo synaptic weights not only based on their current activity levels but also based on these synaptic tags reflecting recent activity.
evidence: This is a description of the model learning mechanism.

claim: Connections from the input to output layers are plastic and learned via supervised learning using the XCAL learning rule.
source: As such the connections from the input to output layers are plastic, and this mapping is learned via supervised learning (i.e. target colors are presented and the network learns from errors using the XCAL learning rule, see appendix).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model training.

claim: Connections from PFC output stripes to the output layer are plastic and learn according to the XCAL rule.
source: As such, connections from PFC output stripes to the output layer are also plastic and learns according to the same rule.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model training.

claim: All networks are trained for 500 epochs and 100 trials per epoch.
source: All networks are trained for 500 epochs and 100 trials per epoch. This was more than sufficient for learning to converge.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model training.

claim: Top-down projections from prefrontal cortex to posterior sites allow networks to bias the sensory representation toward those stored in PFC, facilitating chunking.
source: The base model incorporates purely feedforward visual input that can be stored in prefrontal cortex. But it is widely appreciated that there are also top-down projections from prefrontal cortex to posterior sites (e.g. in parietal cortex). We posited that these top-down projections would allow networks to bias the sensory representation toward those stored in PFC, facilitating chunking.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model mechanism based on known anatomy.

claim: The degree of bias toward PFC representations depends on the strength of top-down projections.
source: The degree of such bias should depend on the strength of those projections, and indeed experimental evidence shows multiple abstractions of an item across parietal cortex and auxiliary sensory regions Ito and Murray, 2023.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to experimental evidence.

claim: The chunking layer receives excitatory input from both sensory regions and top-down information from deep PFC maintenance layers.
source: We considered a minimal set up in which the network has access to two such representations, allowing it to represent both the raw sensory input (through connections directly to PFC) but also via a 'chunking layer' representing posterior cortical association areas that receive excitatory input from both sensory regions and top-down information from deep PFC maintenance layers (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: If any currently maintained PFC representation is close enough to the current sensory input, overlapping neural activations will be enhanced, biasing the chunk layer toward the nearest PFC representation.
source: This convergent excitatory connectivity ensures that if any of the currently maintained PFC representations is close enough to the current sensory input, the overlapping neural activations will be enhanced, thereby biasing the bump attractor in the chunk layer to be attracted toward the nearest PFC representation(s).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Lateral inhibition ensures that only the most excited units will remain active in the chunking layer.
source: Lateral inhibition ensures that only the most excited units will remain active.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: The chunk layer will either represent the original incoming stimulus or a combined representation between the incoming and existing stimuli.
source: As such, the chunk layer will either represent the original incoming stimulus (if no PFC representation is sufficiently close to it) or a combined representation between the incoming and existing stimuli (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: A given PFC stripe receives projections from either the sensory input or the chunking layer.
source: Critically, a given PFC stripe receives projections from either the sensory input or the chunking layer.
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture.

claim: PBWM could learn a gating strategy to store either the original sensory input or the chunked representation.
source: As such, PBWM could learn a gating strategy to store either the original sensory input into the corresponding PFC stripe or to store the chunked representation into the other stripe.
evidence: This is a description of the model learning capability.

claim: For each experiment, at least 80 separate random seeds were run for each network, and results are averaged across them.
source: For each experiment, at least 80 separate random seeds were run for each network, and results are averaged across them.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the simulations.

claim: The models were trained and tested with set sizes 2, 3, or 4.
source: To test how set size affects learning and memory performance, the models were trained and tested with set sizes 2, 3, or 4.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the simulations.

claim: Networks were presented with continuous sensory inputs represented as coarse-coded Gaussian bumps of neural activity in conjunction with their associated discrete orientation.
source: We focus our simulations on variants of the color wheel task (see Methods). Briefly, networks were presented with continuous sensory inputs represented as coarse-coded Gaussian bumps of neural activity in conjunction with their associated discrete orientation.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the simulations.

claim: The error is the difference between the decoded color from the output population and the ground truth value presented during the earlier store trial.
source: The error is then simply the difference between the decoded color from this population and the ground truth value that was presented during the earlier store trial for that orientation.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about error measurement.

claim: If the model outputs an incorrect color that corresponds to a different orientation, this is referred to as a binding or swap error.
source: If the model outputs an incorrect color, but that color corresponds to a different orientation, this is referred to as a binding or swap error (Bays et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a definition of error types supported by citation.

claim: If the response is incorrect and nowhere near any of the colors for the stored orientations, it is referred to as a guess.
source: Finally, if the response is incorrect and nowhere near any of the colors for the stored orientations, it would be referred to as a guess.
evidence: This is a definition of error types.

claim: All models were allocated two PFC maintenance stripes in the minimal setup.
source: For proof of concept, we began with a minimal set-up in which all models were allocated two PFC maintenance stripes (we relax this assumption later to compare to models with larger allocated capacity).
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the model setup.

claim: When set size is equal to the number of stripes (2), errors are small and centered around 0, with similar performance between chunk and no-chunk models.
source: When set size is equal to the number of stripes (2), errors are small and centered around 0, with some variance due to precision. The overall performance is similar between models, but note that the chunk model shows somewhat more imprecise responses as indicated by some more small error trials.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5a.

claim: As set size increases beyond the allocated capacity, both models resort to guessing on a subset of trials.
source: As set size increases beyond the allocated capacity, both models resort to guessing (random errors) on a subset of trials. This pattern is observable by the error histogram containing a mixture of errors centered around zero and a uniform distribution (see Figure 1), as commonly observed in humans (Zhang and Luck, 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5, supported by citation to human data.

claim: The chunking model guesses less than the no chunk model and has a higher chance of precisely recalling items when set size exceeds allocated capacity.
source: Notably, the chunking model guesses less than the no chunk model and has a higher chance of precisely recalling the items (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The difference between the chunk and no chunk model widens as the item limit continues to grow beyond the number of stripes.
source: The difference between the chunk and no chunk model widens as the item limit continues to grow beyond the number of stripes.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: When two items are chunked into one stripe, the second stripe is free to hold another item.
source: In the model, when two items are chunked into one stripe, the second stripe is free to hold another item.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: Chunking should manifest in terms of loss of precision when probed with any of the chunked items, but improved memory for the other items.
source: One key prediction is that chunking should not only manifest in terms of loss of precision when probed with any of the chunked items, but improved memory for the other items (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model mechanism.

claim: When other items in a set are chunkable (low OCV), the chunking network exhibits significantly smaller errors than the control network on the probed item.
source: Indeed, the data supports this prediction (Figure 6). When other items in a set are chunkable (low OCV), the chunking network exhibits significantly smaller errors than the control network on the probed item.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: After some OCV threshold, the chunking network no longer exhibits an advantage, and both networks show increasing errors.
source: After some OCV threshold, the chunking network no longer exhibits an advantage, and both networks show increasing errors.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: When set size is 2, chunk and no-chunk models are equally able to utilize both stripes on 100% of the trials after learning.
source: When the set size is 2, after learning, chunk and no-chunk models are equally able to utilize both stripes on 100% of the trials (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: As set size increases beyond allocated capacity, the no-chunk model's stripe usage actually decreases, and stripes are sometimes empty.
source: When the network attempts to gate information into both stripes, the no-chunk model will often receive negative reward prediction errors during recall trials when it will inevitably be forced to guess for a subset of the stimuli that is not in its allocated memory. As a result, input-gating strategies will be punished, even if they were successfully employed and would have been useful had the other stimuli been probed. In turn, due to punishing gating policies that are generally useful, the stripe usage actually decreases, and the stripes are sometimes empty, akin to 'giving up.'
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7, with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The chunk model is more effective at managing its resources when set size exceeds allocated capacity.
source: In contrast, the chunk model is more effective at managing its resources when set size exceeds allocated capacity (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: As set size increases, the chunk network has more opportunities for chunking and more instances of reinforcing the gating operation linked to the chunk stripe.
source: As set size increases, the network has more opportunities for chunking, and accordingly, relatively more instances of reinforcing the gating operation linked to the chunk stripe.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model mechanism based on analysis of gating patterns.

claim: As set size just exceeds allocated capacity (set size 3), the chunk network decreases its use of the input stripe.
source: Interestingly, as set size just exceeds allocated capacity (here, for set size 3), the network decreases its use of the input stripe.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: As set size increases further (set size 4), the chunk network learns the benefit of storing some items in the held out input stripe, increasing effective capacity.
source: Finally, as set size increases further (set size 4), the chunk network learns the benefit of storing some items in the held out input stripe, increasing effective capacity, while still effectively using the chunk stripe.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 7.

claim: Resource management and utilization is more consequential than the absolute number of stripes available.
source: In sum, this analysis suggests that resource management and utilization is more consequential than the absolute number of stripes available.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: Chunking is an information compression mechanism that allows multiple stimuli to be mapped onto the same stripe.
source: Chunking is an information compression mechanism that allows multiple stimuli to be mapped onto the same stripe.
evidence: This is a description of the chunking mechanism in the model.

claim: The chunk stripe has the advantage of being used repeatedly, giving the network more opportunities to learn how and when to use that stripe.
source: The chunk stripe has the advantage of being used repeatedly, giving the network has more opportunities to learn how and when to use that stripe.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model learning dynamics.

claim: When allocated four stripes for set size 4, chunk networks have more density at zero and low errors compared to no-chunk networks.
source: Indeed, results supported these conclusions. Error distributions in chunk networks have more density at zero and low errors. The chunking model also guesses less (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 8a.

claim: When comparing chunk model with two stripes vs. no chunk model with eight stripes, the chunk model guesses slightly more but has more precise responses.
source: This result largely persisted even in the more extreme case when allocating the control (no-chunk) model 8 stripes (twice as many as needed) and reverting the chunk model to using only two stripes. While guessing is slightly reduced when having more stripes (due to more opportunities to store stimuli), the 8-stripe model does not increase the number of times it precisely recalls the correct item relative to the chunk model with only two stripes (Figure 8b).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The 8-stripe model produced a larger density of moderate errors around the 0–30 degree range.
source: Upon further inspection, one can see that the 8-stripe model produced a larger density of moderate errors around the 0–30 degree range.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 8b.

claim: The 8-stripe network frequently reads out from multiple stripes in parallel during recall (an average of 2.53 stripes).
source: Indeed, we found that the over-extended eight stripe network frequently reads out from (output gates) multiple stripes in parallel (an average of 2.53 stripes during recall), and thus even when the response does reflect the correct item it is also 'contaminated' by reading out one of the other stripes, such that the averaged response results in a larger number of moderate errors.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the model's gating behavior.

claim: The two stripe networks output gated an average of 1.08 stripes for each trial, appropriately reading out from a single PFC representation.
source: In contrast, the two stripe networks (across both no chunk and chunk) output gated an average of 1.08 stripes for each trial, appropriately reading out from a single PFC representation.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the model's gating behavior.

claim: Simply allocating a network with larger numbers of stripes does not yield advantages when gating strategies need to be learned rather than hard-wired.
source: In sum, simply allocating a network with larger numbers of stripes does not yield the naïve advantages one might expect, at least when gating strategies need to be learned rather than hard-wired.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: The large number of input and output gating operations needed for adaptive behavior leads to a credit assignment problem.
source: The large number of input and output gating operations to consider in tandem needed for adaptive behavior leads to a vexing credit assignment problem, as it becomes a challenge to know which of several gating operations or several PFC representations are responsible for task success/error, and networks fall into an unfortunate local minimum.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model learning dynamics.

claim: The credit assignment problem is mitigated by chunking, allowing the network to reinforce the same input and output gating policy across multiple instances.
source: This credit assignment problem is mitigated by chunking, allowing the network to reinforce the same input and output gating policy across multiple instances.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model learning dynamics.

claim: At set size 2, the best performance is along the axis where DA burst and dip gain are symmetrical.
source: The best performance for set size 2 (Figure 10a) is along the axis where burst and dip gain are symmetrical.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 10a.

claim: As set size increases, the best performance is on the axis where burst gain is somewhat greater than the dip gain.
source: As set size increases, the task becomes harder, and rewards are sparser due to more errors. In this case the best performance is on the axis where burst gain is somewhat greater than the dip gain; the model learns best when it can emphasize learning from sparse rewards.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 10b-c.

claim: When set size increases, learning proper gating strategies becomes difficult, and incorrect responses generate negative RPEs that punish preceding gating actions.
source: When set size increases, learning the proper gating strategies becomes difficult. The models may correctly gate a few items in, but they may be incorrectly overwritten or incorrectly output gated at time of recall. Importantly, incorrect responses generate negative RPEs that punish preceding gating actions, even if some of those actions were appropriate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model learning dynamics.

claim: A preponderance of negative RPEs can cause a network to 'give up,' leading to empty stripes.
source: A preponderance of negative RPEs can thus cause a network to 'give up,' as observed in the no-chunk models when set size exceeds allocated capacity, leading to empty stripes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model learning dynamics supported by reference to Figure 7.

claim: The chunk model can combat against using the 'giving-up' strategy because the chunk stripe is used more frequently and has a greater chance of receiving positive reinforcement.
source: The chunk model can combat against using the 'giving-up' strategy: when items are chunked, the chunk stripe is used more frequently and, therefore, has a greater chance of receiving the positive reinforcement, and thus benefits from shared credit assignment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model learning dynamics.

claim: The chunk model still fails if the DA dip value is sufficiently larger than the DA burst.
source: However, the chunk model still fails if the DA dip value is sufficiently larger than the DA burst, for similar 'giving up' reasons (Figure 10c and e).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 10.

claim: The model reproduces recency effects, with average error monotonically increasing with number of intervening trials since the relevant stimulus was encountered.
source: Our network reproduces these effects, with average error monotonically increasing with number of intervening trials since the relevant stimulus was encountered, in both set sizes 3 and 4 (Figure 11).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 11.

claim: Recency effects result from the principle that with more intervening trials, the gating model is more likely to have updated a corresponding stripe.
source: This results from the simple principle whereby with more intervening trials, the gating model is more likely to have updated a corresponding stripe, either replacing it altogether (leading to increased probability of forgetting) or chunking with previous items, thereby increasing average error.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mechanism underlying recency effects in the model.

claim: The errors are overall smaller in set size 3 because the network is less likely to overwrite an item altogether.
source: The errors are overall smaller in set size 3 because the network is less likely to overwrite an item altogether (it can chunk and still recall one of the items perfectly).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results shown in Figure 11.

claim: The recency effects asymptote in set size 4 due to increased opportunities for chunking.
source: Finally, the recency effects asymptotes in set size 4 due to increased opportunities for chunking(indeed, no-chunk networks continued to show increasing errors four trials back; not shown).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model results shown in Figure 11.

claim: The work synthesizes and reconciles theories of visual WM across multiple levels of abstraction.
source: Our work synthesizes and reconciles theories of visual WM across multiple levels of abstraction.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the contribution of the work.

claim: When augmented with continuous population code values and a chunking layer, PBWM comprises a hybrid between slots and resources with resource-like constraints within individual stripes.
source: Here, we show that when augmented with continuous population code values and a chunking layer, PBWM comprises a hybrid between slots and resources with resource-like constraints within individual stripes.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's properties.

claim: Through reinforcement learning, adaptive gating policies can adjust the degree to which behavior mimics primarily slots-like or resource-like as a function of task demands.
source: Moreover, through reinforcement learning, adaptive gating policies can adjust the degree to which behavior mimics primarily slots-like or resource-like as a function task demands.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's learning capabilities.

claim: The model accounts for human findings supporting chunking of related items in WM, that such chunking evolves with reward feedback, and is predictive of better performance with increasing task demands.
source: As such, this model accounts for human findings supporting chunking of related items in WM, that such chunking evolves with reward feedback, and is predictive of better performance with increasing task demands across multiple datasets (Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's ability to account for human data.

claim: PBWM is ostensibly a slot-like model with distinct PFC clusters corresponding to slots that can be independently gated.
source: On its surface, PBWM is ostensibly a slot-like model, with distinct PFC clusters ('stripes') corresponding to slots that can be independently gated, giving rise to useful computational properties such as variable binding, indirection, compositionality, and hierarchical generalization (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006; Kriete et al., 2013; Collins and Frank, 2013; Calderon et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a characterization of PBWM supported by citations.

claim: The need for gating accords with data suggesting that effective WM capacity is related to management of WM content and one's ability to filter out distractors.
source: The need for gating also accords with data suggesting that effective WM capacity is related to management of WM content, ie. one's ability to filter out distractors so as to prioritize task-relevant information Vogel et al., 2005; Astle et al., 2014; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Vogel, 2019, and that such abilities rely on basal ganglia output and function (McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Baier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's consistency with empirical data, supported by citations.

claim: In the augmented PBWM, chunking is not obligatory, as the network can learn a gating policy that prioritizes raw sensory inputs or to replace a currently stored PFC item with the chunk.
source: However, in our network, this layer receives bottom-up input from both the sensory input layer and top-down input from all the PFC stripes, thereby allowing the network to combine sensory information with the nearest neighbor in memory. Moreover, WM chunking in our model is not obligatory, as the network can learn a gating policy that prioritizes raw sensory inputs (in which case it can represent a given item precisely) or to either replace a currently stored PFC item with the chunked version.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: The PBWM-chunk model can learn to store more items than the allocated slots capacity by combining representations while incurring the cost of lost precision on the chunked items.
source: As such, the PBWM-chunk model can learn to store more items than the allocated slots capacity by combining representations while incurring the cost of lost precision on the chunked items, giving rise to resource-like behavior.
evidence: This is a description of the model's capabilities.

claim: The model addresses key limitations in previous neural models where chunking was obligatory and could not be optimized.
source: As such, our model addresses key limitations in previous neural models in this domain, in which chunking was obligatory fashion due to perceptual overlap and could not be optimized (Wei et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's advantages over previous models.

claim: PBWM adapts whether or not to chunk as a function of task demands and reward history, similar to empirical data.
source: Instead, PBWM adapts whether or not to chunk as a function of task demands and reward history (Figure 9), similar to empirical data (Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations shown in Figure 9, compared to empirical data.

claim: PBWM can report only the color of the probed item, unlike previous neural models which were considered accurate as long as the probed color was one of the various populations still active.
source: Furthermore, PBWM can also report only the color of the probed item, unlike previous neural models which were considered accurate as long as the probed color was one of the various populations still active (Wei et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's advantages over previous models.

claim: To perform adequately, PBWM requires learning appropriate input and output gating policies which are not hard-wired and involves solving a difficult credit assignment problem.
source: Critically, to perform adequately, PBWM requires learning appropriate input and output gating policies which are not hard-wired, and indeed involves solving a difficult credit assignment problem (O'Reilly and Frank, 2006).
evidence: This is a description of the model's learning requirements.

claim: Using a smaller number of stripes but allowing for chunking provides a lossy compression strategy that can mitigate the credit assignment problem.
source: As such, using a smaller number of stripes but allowing for chunking provides a lossy compression strategy that can mitigate this problem and render credit assignment easier, despite the loss of precision.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model's learning advantages.

claim: The simulations provide understanding that WM capacity limitations result from properly utilizing and managing resources to optimize performance rather than limits in the number of neurons or stripes available.
source: As such, our simulations provide a provocative if somewhat speculative understanding of the nature of WM capacity limitations. It is unlikely that such limitations result from limits in the number of neurons or stripes available in prefrontal cortex, given that discrete estimates on capacity limitations range in the order of three to four items whereas the number of stripes (or equivalent clusters of PFC populations) is orders of magnitude larger (Frank et al., 2001). Our simulations show that a limiting step is properly utilizing and managing resources to optimize performance (Figure 7), and that it might actually be more effective to limit the number of representations used.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model results.

claim: The limitation in the model is not simply about number of slots but the complexity of learning.
source: Increasing model capacity to four and eight stripes and the resulting comparisons show that the limitation in the model is not simply about number of slots but the complexity of learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model simulations.

claim: Using WM requires multiple input and output gating decisions and strategies in tandem with solving and learning a task.
source: Using WM requires multiple input and output gating decisions and strategies in tandem with solving and learning a task - this would become trivial with a homunculus dictating what information to store and where to store it. In biology, the PFC has to learn these gating strategies: it is not hardwired.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the nature of WM in biological systems.

claim: The findings accord with data showing that effective WM capacity is about the ability to filter out irrelevant information, the importance of the task (reward), and experience with the task.
source: This set of experiments helps explain various other WM findings which suggest that effective WM capacity is not just about 'capacity' but rather is also about the ability to filter out irrelevant information, the importance of the task (reward), and experience with the task (experts vs. novice) (McNab and Klingberg, 2008; Astle et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2018; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Vogel, 2019; Nakajima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the model's consistency with empirical findings, supported by citations.

claim: When exceeding capacity, networks often 'gave up' with more trials having at least one stripe empty, due to negative prediction errors punishing gating policies.
source: It also accords with our findings that when exceeding capacity, networks often 'gave up' in the sense that they had more trials in which at least one stripe was empty, due to the influence of negative prediction errors punishing gating policies.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: Networks require a larger dopamine burst than dip to succeed with increasing task demands.
source: As such, we showed that networks require a larger dopamine burst than dip to succeed with increasing task demands.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations.

claim: The finding that networks require larger DA burst than dip accords with data in rodents showing that dopamine depletion can cause progressive 'unlearning' of adaptive strategies via aberrant NoGo learning.
source: This finding also accords with related data in rodents and our network model in the motor domain, whereby dopamine depletion can cause a progressive 'unlearning' of adaptive strategies (i.e. 'giving up') via aberrant NoGo learning (Beeler et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison of the model results with empirical data, supported by citation.

claim: Learned Parkinsonism was shown to be related to plasticity in D2 medium spiny neurons and depends on the indirect pathway.
source: This learned Parkinsonism was shown to be related to plasticity in D2 medium spiny neurons (Beeler et al., 2012), and this mechanism was recently confirmed to depend on the indirect pathway (Cheung et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Dopamine is a critical component of RL by adjusting synaptic weights into striatal modules that support input and output gating.
source: In the network, dopamine is a critical component of RL by adjusting synaptic weights into striatal modules that support input and output gating.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: The need for a healthy balanced dynamic range of DA signals for adaptive performance provides a potential mechanism to explain deficits in patient populations with altered striatal DA signaling.
source: The need for a healthy balanced dynamic range of DA signals for adaptive performance provides a potential window into a mechanism that can explain deficits in patient populations with altered striatal DA signaling.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model results with implications for patient populations.

claim: Altered DA signaling in patient populations with schizophrenia and ADHD could influence chunking and efficient use of resources.
source: Whereas much of the literature in patients with schizophrenia and ADHD focuses on limitations in WM capacity, our simulations suggest an alternative whereby altered DA signaling in these populations (Maia and Frank, 2017) could influence chunking and efficient use of resources.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model results with implications for patient populations, supported by citation.

claim: Adaptively learned gating policies are important for controlling when and whether to chunk, which may have implications for patient populations with repetitive negative thinking.
source: Our finding that adaptively learned gating policies are important for controlling when and whether to chunk may have implications for recent accounts of patient populations with repetitive negative thinking, which are proposed to arise from failures inherent to learning adaptive mental gating (Hitchcock and Frank, 2024).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model results with implications for patient populations, supported by citation.
